summary: Ahead of the second in-person meeting between Joe Biden and Xi Jinping in San Francisco, the article describes U.S.-China relations as focused on crisis prevention after a tense year. Analysts expect dialogue and possible cooperation on AI and humanitarian issues, but export controls and Taiwan remain major friction points and trust is low. Goodwill steps such as resumed flights and agricultural deals have improved the atmosphere, though no substantive changes have occurred.
one_line: Biden and Xi's San Francisco summit aims to stabilize strained U.S.-China ties and prevent crisis, though export controls, Taiwan and low trust persist.
key_facts: Biden and Xi Jinping are set to meet in person for the second time since Biden took office, on Wednesday in San Francisco alongside the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting.
Michael Hirson of 22V Research said the focus will be on expanding dialogue to lower tail risks and prevent a crisis neither leader is looking for.
An alleged Chinese spy balloon in U.S. airspace in early February pushed the two countries to suspend already limited high-level talks.
In April, the Center for Strategic and International Studies described U.S.-China relations as seemingly 'caught in a worsening vicious cycle.'
Antony Blinken made a high-stakes visit to Beijing in June, and in early October Chuck Schumer and five other senators had an 80-minute meeting with Xi.
Shen Yamei of the China Institute of International Studies said the easing is a relaxation of the atmosphere and 'No actual changes have occurred.'
Gina Raimondo 'said no' in August to China's requests to reduce U.S. export controls, calling them 'matters of national security.'
Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng raised export controls and investment restrictions with Janet Yellen in San Francisco on Nov. 10, according to state media.
Gabriel Wildau of Teneo said the meeting is likely to mark a cyclical high point and the window of opportunity for stabilizing relations since June may close afterward.
Taiwan holds a presidential election in January 2024, and a more pro-independence winner could stir Beijing's ire.
Nancy Pelosi in August 2021 became the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit Taiwan in 25 years, prompting Beijing to suspend climate talks with the U.S.
Wildau suggested the leaders might pledge cooperation on safe AI use, humanitarian aid to Gaza, grain passage through the Black Sea, and postwar reconstruction.
Chinese commodity importers in October signed the first agreements since 2017 to buy U.S. agricultural products in bulk.
The three remaining giant pandas on loan from Beijing returned to China last week due to an expiring contract.
